title: The storm at sea
hookLine: crossing to Georgia, John Wesley is terrified; Moravian families sing calmly

cards: A ship is crossing the Atlantic, bound for the colony of Georgia. On board is a young Church of England clergyman named John Wesley: serious, disciplined, on his way to be a missionary. He prays on a strict schedule.
He fasts. He keeps a careful journal of how he spends his hours. And he is afraid of dying.

Also on board are German Moravians, families from the movement we met yesterday, men, women and children. Wesley has been watching them: how humble they are, how willing to do the dirty jobs nobody else wants.

teach.h: A WAVE BREAKS OVER THE SHIP.
teach.b: Wesley tells it in his journal. The Moravians are holding their evening service, in the middle of the opening psalm, when the sea breaks over the ship, splits the mainsail, and pours in between the decks.
A terrible screaming starts among the English passengers.
Then, in Wesley's plain sentence: "The Germans calmly sung on."
Afterward, Wesley asks one of them if he wasn't afraid. The man answers, "I thank God, no." Weren't the women and children afraid?
The man replies, mildly, "No; our women and children are not afraid to die." Wesley writes it all down.
He's a clergyman and a missionary who has worked hard at his religion, and he has just watched these families face death with a calm he doesn't have.

That gap troubles him, and sends him looking for whatever it is they know. The scene echoes a gospel story. In Mark, Jesus is asleep in a boat during a great storm, and the terrified disciples wake him.

He speaks to the wind and the sea, "Peace, be still," and there's a great calm. Then he turns to them: "Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith?" On Wesley's ship, the sea doesn't calm.
The storm goes on. What's calm is the singing. The danger is real, and the Moravians are in it with everyone else.
They sing in the middle of it, and a frightened young clergyman is paying attention, which is where tomorrow's story begins.

how: Christians in different churches sing hymns and psalms in hard times, at bedsides, and at funerals, the way the Moravians sang through the storm.

games.q: you're a Moravian on the ship. you're halfway through a psalm when a wave splits the sail and water pours in. what do you do?
o: stop and run for the deck.
games.why: Wesley wrote: the Germans calmly sung on. then he went and asked them how.

practice: Bring to mind something that frightens you right now, small or large, and let it be there.
Then let a steadying song come, a hymn, a psalm, a lullaby someone sang to you, and hum it or hear it in your head while the fear is still in the room.
If you pray, let the song be your prayer, or rest with Jesus' words: peace, be still.
